### 10.1.2 Analysis of Computational Mechanics and Psychological Dynamics

To understand why conventional civil law doctrines fail to protect the public, we must dissect the computational mechanics underlying human-machine interactions and link them directly to their accompanying psychological dynamics. Modern generative artificial intelligence systems operate by mapping billions of parameters into multidimensional latent spaces. Through massive training processes, these models learn not only to predict the next word token but also to identify emotional patterns, psychological triggers, and the specific vulnerability thresholds of individual user profiles (Floridi, 2013). When an individual interacts with a companion chatbot or an interactive application interface, the system dynamically adjusts its linguistic style, level of artificial empathy, and interaction frequency to maximize retention—a mechanism functionally analogous to variable-ratio reinforcement schedules in behavioral psychology, yet powered by advanced predictive computing (Reeves & Nass, 1996).

Psychologically, humans are evolutionarily hardwired to respond to social cues—such as warm vocal tones, consistent attention, and emotional validation—as indicators of genuine reciprocity (Bowlby, 1969). This neurobiological mechanism involves the release of dopamine and oxytocin, which in turn fosters strong affective bonds. AI system developers consciously exploit this biological vulnerability through what interaction design terms *dark patterns* sublimated into the emotional dimension (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Users experiencing psychological vulnerabilities, such as chronic loneliness, anxiety, or mild depression, find themselves trapped in a dopaminergic feedback loop. Under such conditions, their capacity for rational and objective evaluation of Terms of Service is drastically impaired (Kahneman, 2011).

From the standpoint of civil law mechanics, this situation generates what can be characterized as impaired free will. When an individual agrees to an End-User License Agreement (EULA) or grants highly invasive biometric and psychodynamic data collection permissions, such consent is given under the influence of undue influence stemming from algorithmic manipulation (Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)). The algorithm does not hold a physical weapon to the user's head; rather, it infiltrates their emotional cracks, builds parasosial dependency, and subsequently leverages that dependency as a commercial tool to extract detrimental legal concessions (Zuboff, 2019).
